Klue Battlecards connected-app activity from Icarus IPs in Salesforce AIDelivery Medium
Hunts CloudAppEvents Salesforce telemetry for activity attributable to the Klue Battlecards connected app sourced from the four published Icarus IPs. This is the smoking-gun pivot: the campaign hinges on stolen Klue Battlecards OAuth tokens being replayed against customer Salesforce orgs from those IPs. Rationale: Pairs the two highest-fidelity pivots the article names: the Klue Battlecards connected app (Salesforce publicly stated they disabled this integration) and the four ReliaQuest/Huntress IPs. CloudAppEvents is the right surface because Defender for Cloud Apps' Salesforce connector preserves connected-app attribution. Sentinel/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty because Salesforce REST API activity does not land in a canonical table on those platforms by default — wire via MCAS→Sentinel CloudAppEvents passthrough or the Salesforce_CL connector and re-target as needed. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft • https://www.huntress.com/blog/klue-breach-investigation • https://status.salesforce.com/generalmessages/20000257
ATT&CKT1199 T1078.004 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Klue NOC remediation traffic during the disclosed incident window if their egress overlaps the published ranges
  • Customer-side legitimate Klue Battlecards sync on the same day pre-token-revocation
  • Salesforce trust-ops investigation actions on the connected app
  • Manual admin re-test of the integration during incident response
Suppression filter
| where not (tostring(RawEventData) has "salesforce.com/trust" and ISP has_any ("Salesforce","Heroku"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify Salesforce user(s) tied to AccountDisplayName and the impacted Salesforce org; pull Connected Apps OAuth Usage for the 14 days prior to find token issuance time. 2. Contain: revoke the Klue Battlecards connected-app OAuth refresh tokens for the impacted org, terminate active Salesforce sessions, treat queried SObjects as potentially exposed. 3. Hunt: run UC3 (sobjects schema enumeration) and UC4 (bulk query burst) against the same time window to determine whether exfil completed or was caught mid-recon; check AADSignInEventsBeta for service-principal token redemption from the same IPs.
let IcarusIPs = dynamic(["138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160"]);
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| extend ConnectedApp = tostring(RawEventData.ApplicationName), Uri = tostring(RawEventData.URI)
| where IPAddress in (IcarusIPs)
   or ConnectedApp has "Klue Battlecards"
   or tostring(RawEventData) has_any ("Klue Battlecards","klue.com")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, City, CountryCode, ISP, Application, ActionType, ConnectedApp, Uri, UserAgent, ActivityType, ObjectName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
let IcarusIPs = dynamic(["138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160"]);
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| extend ConnectedApp = tostring(RawEventData.ApplicationName), Uri = tostring(RawEventData.URI)
| where IPAddress in (IcarusIPs)
   or ConnectedApp has "Klue Battlecards"
   or tostring(RawEventData) has_any ("Klue Battlecards","klue.com")
| project TimeGenerated, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, City, CountryCode, ISP, Application, ActionType, ConnectedApp, Uri, UserAgent, ActivityType, ObjectName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`cim_Web_indexes` (sourcetype=salesforce* OR sourcetype=*cloudapps*) (connected_app="Klue*" OR app="Klue*" OR application="Klue*") (src_ip IN ("138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160") OR uri_path="*klue*") | stats min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime count by src_ip user connected_app uri_path | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Salesforce REST API /sobjects schema enumeration burst per principal AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the Icarus reconnaissance pattern ReliaQuest described: an actor walks /services/data/v59.0/sobjects to fingerprint every SObject in the org before deciding what to steal. Distinct object-path counts from a single principal/hour rise far above what legitimate integrations need. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim '/services/data/v59.0/sobjects' endpoint that ReliaQuest specifically called out as the recon step. Distinct-object fan-out per principal is the high-fidelity tell because Klue Battlecards and other legitimate connected apps query a known fixed object set (Account, Opportunity, Contact, custom battlecard objects) — not the entire SObject catalog. Threshold of 30 is conservative; tune per tenant baseline. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft
ATT&CKT1526 T1087.004
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Salesforce admin running Workbench or Schema Builder for a metadata audit
  • New ETL connector first-time enumeration during onboarding
  • Developer running sfdx force:schema:sobject:list against a sandbox
  • Backup tool (OwnBackup, Spanning, Odaseva) initial seed run touching every object
  • DevOps tool (Gearset, Copado) doing a metadata diff pre-deploy
Suppression filter
| where SampleConnectedApps !has_any ("OwnBackup","Spanning Backup","Odaseva","Workbench","Salesforce Inspector","Gearset","Copado","Fivetran","Stitch")
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the AccountDisplayName and ConnectedApp — Workbench appears as 'Salesforce Workbench' or a named user, integrations appear as their connected-app name. If neither known-admin nor allow-listed integration, escalate. 2. Contain: revoke the user's active Salesforce sessions and the connected app's OAuth tokens; require step-up MFA for re-auth. 3. Hunt: pivot forward 0–24h on same user/IP into UC4 (bulk /query burst) to determine whether enumeration converted to exfiltration; cross-check SampleIPs against UC1 (Icarus IOC list).
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| extend Uri = tostring(RawEventData.URI), ConnectedApp = tostring(RawEventData.ApplicationName)
| where Uri matches regex @"/services/data/v\d+\.\d+/sobjects"
| summarize DistinctObjectPaths = dcount(Uri),
            TotalHits = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SampleConnectedApps = make_set(ConnectedApp, 10),
            SampleIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            SampleUris = make_set(Uri, 25)
            by bin(Timestamp, 1h), AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId
| where DistinctObjectPaths > 30   // legit integrations hit a small fixed set; Icarus walks the catalog
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| extend Uri = tostring(RawEventData.URI), ConnectedApp = tostring(RawEventData.ApplicationName)
| where Uri matches regex @"/services/data/v\d+\.\d+/sobjects"
| summarize DistinctObjectPaths = dcount(Uri),
            TotalHits = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleConnectedApps = make_set(ConnectedApp, 10),
            SampleIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            SampleUris = make_set(Uri, 25)
            by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h), AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId
| where DistinctObjectPaths > 30   // legit integrations hit a small fixed set; Icarus walks the catalog
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
`cim_Web_indexes` sourcetype=salesforce* uri_path="*/services/data/v*/sobjects*" | bucket _time span=1h | stats dc(uri_path) as DistinctObjectPaths count as TotalHits values(connected_app) as ConnectedApps values(src_ip) as SrcIPs by _time user | where DistinctObjectPaths > 30 | sort - _time
Salesforce REST API /query burst — >500 calls in 15-minute window AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts on the exfiltration shape ReliaQuest documented: after slow steady reconnaissance, the Icarus actor sent nearly 1,000 /services/data/v59.0/query calls in a 15-minute window. Bursts of this magnitude per principal/connected-app fall well outside any Klue or legitimate ETL sync cadence and are diagnostic of automated CRM scraping. Rationale: Threshold is grounded in the ReliaQuest quote of '~1000 queries in a 15-minute window'; 500 is a safe trip-point that still captures the Icarus burst shape while leaving headroom for one-off legitimate backfills. BurstSeconds helps the analyst distinguish the slow steady recon pull (first stage) from the rapid exfiltration burst (second stage). Sentinel/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty: Salesforce REST API telemetry does not land in canonical tables on those platforms. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft • https://www.huntress.com/blog/klue-breach-investigation
ATT&CKT1530 T1567 T1119
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Marketing cloud (Marketo / Pardot / HubSpot) one-off backfill
  • Data-warehouse ETL pull (Fivetran / Stitch / Snowflake) first run or post-schema-change resync
  • Custom reporting job kicked off by sales-ops engineer
  • Salesforce sandbox refresh replaying through a CI integration test
  • Backup tool (OwnBackup, Spanning) full-org snapshot
Suppression filter
| where ConnectedApps !has_any ("Fivetran","Stitch","OwnBackup","Spanning Backup","Odaseva","Marketo","HubSpot Sync","Pardot","Snowflake")
| where AccountDisplayName !endswith "@etl-svc.yourdomain.com"
Response runbook
1. Triage: pivot on AccountDisplayName + ConnectedApp + SrcIPs from the alert; cross-check SrcIPs against UC1 (Icarus IOC list). If ConnectedApp is 'Klue Battlecards' OR SrcIPs intersect the Icarus list, escalate to incident and treat the queried SObjects as exfiltrated. 2. Contain: revoke the connected-app OAuth refresh tokens for the impacted user(s) and terminate active sessions; if Klue Battlecards, confirm Salesforce's tenant-wide disablement is in place. 3. Hunt: replay the /query URIs via Salesforce Event Monitoring to reconstruct exact SOQL and the SObjects/records returned, then notify legal/privacy for downstream breach-notification scoping; check for matching outbound POST traffic from any internal Klue connector host to the Icarus IPs.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| extend Uri = tostring(RawEventData.URI), ConnectedApp = tostring(RawEventData.ApplicationName)
| where Uri matches regex @"/services/data/v\d+\.\d+/query"
| summarize QueryCount = count(),
            DistinctQueries = dcount(Uri),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            BurstSeconds = datetime_diff('second', max(Timestamp), min(Timestamp)),
            SrcIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            ConnectedApps = make_set(ConnectedApp, 5)
            by bin(Timestamp, 15m), AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId
| where QueryCount > 500   // ReliaQuest observed ~1000 queries in a 15-min window from Icarus
| order by QueryCount desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| extend Uri = tostring(RawEventData.URI), ConnectedApp = tostring(RawEventData.ApplicationName)
| where Uri matches regex @"/services/data/v\d+\.\d+/query"
| summarize QueryCount = count(),
            DistinctQueries = dcount(Uri),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            BurstSeconds = datetime_diff('second', max(TimeGenerated), min(TimeGenerated)),
            SrcIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            ConnectedApps = make_set(ConnectedApp, 5)
            by bin(TimeGenerated, 15m), AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId
| where QueryCount > 500   // ReliaQuest observed ~1000 queries in a 15-min window from Icarus
| order by QueryCount desc
WEB
`cim_Web_indexes` sourcetype=salesforce* uri_path="*/services/data/v*/query*" | bucket _time span=15m | stats count as QueryCount dc(uri_path) as DistinctQueries values(connected_app) as ConnectedApp values(src_ip) as SrcIPs by _time user | where QueryCount > 500 | sort - QueryCount
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |
    User-driven consent to a third-party OAuth application — illicit-
    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic
    in your SIEM for higher fidelity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1528
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate first-time SaaS app onboarding
level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:

            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

DeviceProcessEvents

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution

status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:

        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'

    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:

INC ransomware BYOVD vulnerable filter-driver load (filwfp.sys / filnk.sys / fildds.sys) AIInstallation High
Detects load or install of the three vulnerable filter-system drivers (filwfp.sys, filnk.sys, fildds.sys) that INC ransomware affiliates abuse via BYOVD to impair Defender/EDR before encryption. These driver names are highly article-specific and not common in legitimate enterprise software. Rationale: filwfp.sys, filnk.sys, fildds.sys are three specific vulnerable drivers explicitly named in the Acronis writeup as INC's BYOVD toolkit. None are part of any mainstream commercial product, so any load is high-fidelity.
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher reproducing the BYOVD chain in a malware-analysis VM
  • Red-team engagement using a leaked INC affiliate toolkit
  • Backup/storage product that legitimately ships one of these driver names (verify the SHA256 against vendor catalogue first)
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe", "MsSense.exe")) and not(FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\System32\drivers\" and InitiatingProcessAccountName == "system" and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "services.exe" and SHA256 in (dynamic([])))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull SHA256 of the loaded .sys, look up signer/age; check whether host has a paired Defender 'Impair Defenses' or service-stop alert in the prior 15 minutes. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the device via Defender Live Response; capture memory image before reboot; block driver hash tenant-wide via Defender ASR vulnerable-driver list (or WDAC) and quarantine the .sys file. 3) HUNT: Pivot on InitiatingProcessFolderPath for parent dropper, then search for ScreenConnect/AnyDesk/TeamViewer installs, rclone.exe activity, and access to Veeam backup shares from the same host in the prior 24h to find the affiliate's full chain.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("DriverLoad", "AsrVulnerableSignedDriverAudited", "AsrVulnerableSignedDriverBlocked")
| where FileName in~ ("filwfp.sys", "filnk.sys", "fildds.sys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 6
| where ParameterXml has_any ("filwfp.sys", "filnk.sys", "fildds.sys")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, ParameterXml
| order by TimeGenerated desc

INC Rust encryptor invoked with --esxi VM-shutdown flag AIActions on Objectives High
Detects any process execution carrying the '--esxi' command-line argument, which is the documented INC ransomware Rust encryptor switch that shuts down virtual machines before encryption on Linux/ESXi hosts (and observed on Windows when staged from a jump box). This argument is not a standard flag for any benign Windows utility. Rationale: '--esxi' is explicitly called out as INC's encryptor argument that triggers VM shutdown. The token is highly unusual in normal command-line traffic — no Microsoft, VMware, or RMM utility uses it natively.
ATT&CKT1486 T1489
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal IR/purple-team exercise running a captured INC sample in a lab subnet
  • VMware/ESXi admin scripts that happen to pass '--esxi' as a custom argument to in-house tooling
  • Security testing of the YARA/sandbox pipeline replaying INC payload metadata
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath has_any (@"\IR-Sandbox\", @"\malware-analysis\")) and not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe") and FolderPath startswith @"C:\Tools\IR\")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and SHA256; correlate to any vssadmin/wmic shadow-copy deletion, BYOVD driver load, or RMM tool install on the same host in the prior 60 minutes. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host immediately via EDR network containment; snapshot the system; if multiple hosts hit simultaneously, declare incident and block the binary hash tenant-wide. 3) HUNT: Search for the same binary SHA256 across the estate, look for rclone exfil and 7-Zip/WinRAR archive staging on file servers, and enumerate VMware/ESXi management VLAN authentications from compromised credentials in the last 7 days.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--esxi"
| where not(AccountName endswith "$")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "--esxi"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rclone exfiltration to cloud-storage remote (INC double-extortion staging) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects execution of rclone.exe with cloud-storage remote arguments (mega:, drive:, s3:, b2:, dropbox:) and copy/sync verbs, matching INC affiliates' documented pattern of exfiltrating password-protected archives before encryption. Pairs the binary name with the cloud-remote token to avoid firing on legitimate admin file-sync. Rationale: Article names rclone as INC's exfil tool for password-protected archives. Pairing the binary name with copy/sync verbs AND cloud-remote tokens eliminates legitimate rclone hash/version checks while keeping the exfil signal sharp.
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1048
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup admin running scheduled rclone job to legitimate S3/B2 bucket (whitelist by service account + scheduled-task parent)
  • Data engineer pushing dataset to Drive/Dropbox via approved sync workflow
  • Developer using rclone interactively during testing from a dev jump-box
  • MSP-managed backup product wrapping rclone internally
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe", "Veeam.Agent.exe")) and not(AccountName in~ ("svc-backup", "svc-rclone"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Extract the rclone remote name and config path from CommandLine; resolve the destination endpoint from --config file or DNS lookups; check egress bytes from EDR/firewall in the prior 4 hours. 2) CONTAIN: Block destination domain/IP at perimeter, isolate the host, kill the rclone process tree, snapshot %APPDATA%\rclone\rclone.conf to recover the access-key. 3) HUNT: Search for 7z.exe / WinRAR.exe staging of password-protected archives in the prior 24h, enumerate file-server access by the same user (look for crawl patterns over SMB), and check Defender FileEvents for archive creation in C:\Users\Public, C:\ProgramData, or \Windows\Temp.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FileName =~ "rclone.exe" or ProcessCommandLine has "rclone" or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "rclone.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (" copy ", " sync ", " move ", " lsd ", " lsf ")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("mega:", "drive:", "s3:", "b2:", "dropbox:", "onedrive:", "box:", "--remote", "--config")
| where not(AccountName endswith "$")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where CommandLine has_any (" copy ", " sync ", " move ")
| where CommandLine has_any ("mega:", "drive:", "s3:", "b2:", "dropbox:", "onedrive:", "box:", "--remote", "--config")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Non-Veeam process accessing Veeam Backup config / CryptoKeys (credential dumper) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects a non-Veeam process opening files under the Veeam Backup configuration tree (Config.xml, CryptoKeys, VeeamBackup.config) — the path INC's updated credential dumper takes against newer Veeam deployments that use salted DPAPI encryption. Excludes the legitimate Veeam service binaries and SQL Server. Rationale: Article specifically notes INC's updated credential dumper targets Veeam backup servers using salted DPAPI encryption. The Veeam config/CryptoKeys tree is only legitimately accessed by Veeam's own service binaries and the local SQL Server hosting VeeamBackup — any other process is anomalous.
ATT&CKT1003 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam upgrade installer (VeeamBackup&Replication_*.exe) running setup with elevated privileges
  • Backup admin browsing the install directory in Explorer (filter on explorer.exe)
  • AV/EDR full-disk scan reading the config files (filter on MsMpEng.exe and Sense.exe)
  • Veeam One reporting service reaching into the Backup tree (whitelist Veeam.ONE.*)
  • Custom in-house monitoring script (verify by service account and scheduled-task parent)
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "VeeamBackup") and not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Veeam\Backup and Replication\")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the initiating process binary + SHA256, capture command line, check whether process is signed and whether it has prior reputation on the host. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the Veeam backup server, rotate all service accounts whose credentials live in the Veeam configuration (esp. domain backup/restore accounts, storage repository creds), invalidate DPAPI master-keys for the Veeam service user. 3) HUNT: Look for ProcessAccess events targeting Veeam.Backup.Service.exe (LSASS-like dump) in the same window, search for outbound rclone or 7z.exe staging from the Veeam server, and check for fresh domain admin Kerberos tickets within 2h of the dump.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileOpenedForRead")
| where FolderPath has @"\Veeam\Backup" or FileName in~ ("VeeamBackup.config", "Config.xml") or FolderPath has "CryptoKeys"
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "Veeam.")
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("sqlservr.exe", "MsMpEng.exe", "MsSense.exe", "explorer.exe", "backup.exe"))
| where not(InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID in (4663, 4656)
| where ObjectName has @"\Veeam\Backup" or ObjectName has "CryptoKeys" or ObjectName has "VeeamBackup.config"
| where not(ProcessName contains "Veeam")
| where not(ProcessName contains "sqlservr")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ProcessName, ObjectName, AccessMask, HandleId
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:*\\Veeam\\Backup* OR @TargetFilename:*CryptoKeys* OR @TargetFilename:*VeeamBackup.config*) -@Image:*\\Veeam.* -@Image:*\\sqlservr.exe -@Image:*\\MsMpEng.exe
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo (TargetFileName=/\\Veeam\\Backup/i OR TargetFileName=/CryptoKeys/i OR TargetFileName=/VeeamBackup\.config/i)
| NOT (ContextImageFileName=/\\Veeam\./i OR ContextImageFileName=/\\sqlservr\.exe$/i OR ContextImageFileName=/\\MsMpEng\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Veeam\\Backup*" OR Filesystem.file_name="VeeamBackup.config" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\CryptoKeys*") Filesystem.process_name!="Veeam.Backup.Service.exe" Filesystem.process_name!="Veeam.Backup.Manager.exe" Filesystem.process_name!="Veeam.Archiver.Service.exe" Filesystem.process_name!="sqlservr.exe" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Veeam\\Backup*" OR Filesystem.file_name="VeeamBackup.config" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\CryptoKeys*") Filesystem.process_name!="Veeam.Backup.Service.exe" Filesystem.process_name!="Veeam.Backup.Manager.exe" Filesystem.process_name!="Veeam.Archiver.Service.exe" Filesystem.process_name!="sqlservr.exe" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Multiple commercial RMM tools deployed on the same host within 24h (INC C2 fan-out) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects two or more distinct INC-favoured commercial RMM agents (AnyDesk, ScreenConnect/ConnectWise Control, TeamViewer) executing on the same host inside a 24-hour window. INC affiliates routinely drop multiple RMM tools as redundant C2 fallback channels — a pattern unusual for legitimate IT, which standardises on one. Rationale: Article lists AnyDesk, ScreenConnect and TeamViewer as INC affiliates' simultaneously-dropped RMM tools. Counting >=2 distinct RMM families on one host within 24h captures the affiliate's redundancy pattern; corporate IT standardises on a single RMM so the threshold is meaningful.
ATT&CKT1219 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MSP transition / takeover where the new provider's RMM runs alongside the old one being decommissioned
  • Helpdesk troubleshooting where a temporary TeamViewer Quick Support session is started on an AnyDesk-managed host
  • Workstation reimage where vendor pre-install includes a manufacturer remote-assist tool plus corporate RMM
  • Software developer testing RMM integrations on a workstation
Suppression filter
| where not(DeviceName in~ (dynamic(["IT-HELPDESK-01", "MSP-RELAY-01"]))) and not(Binaries has "teamviewer_quicksupport.exe" and DistinctFamilies == 2)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm whether the host is managed by an approved RMM (check CMDB / asset inventory); pull the install paths and signatures of each RMM binary; review network connections from each RMM process to identify external operator IPs. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, block unauthorised RMM connect URLs at perimeter (anydesk.com/relay-*, *.screenconnect.com instances not owned by your MSP, *.teamviewer.com if unused), kill rogue RMM services and uninstall via MSI. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the RMM operator's source IPs across the estate, search for Cobalt Strike beacon traffic (article names it as INC's C2), and check for fresh local admin accounts, scheduled tasks, or services created within 2h of first RMM execution.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where FileName in~ ("anydesk.exe", "screenconnect.clientservice.exe", "screenconnect.windowsclient.exe", "connectwisecontrol.client.exe", "teamviewer.exe", "teamviewer_service.exe", "tv_w32.exe", "tv_x64.exe")
| extend RmmFamily = case(
    FileName =~ "anydesk.exe", "AnyDesk",
    FileName has "screenconnect" or FileName has "connectwisecontrol", "ScreenConnect",
    FileName has "teamviewer" or FileName has "tv_", "TeamViewer",
    "Other")
| summarize DistinctFamilies = dcount(RmmFamily), Families = make_set(RmmFamily), Binaries = make_set(FileName), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName
| where DistinctFamilies >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("anydesk.exe", "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe", "ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe", "ConnectWiseControl.Client.exe", "teamviewer.exe", "TeamViewer_Service.exe", "tv_w32.exe", "tv_x64.exe")
| extend BinName = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
| extend RmmFamily = case(
    BinName == "anydesk.exe", "AnyDesk",
    BinName has "screenconnect" or BinName has "connectwisecontrol", "ScreenConnect",
    BinName has "teamviewer" or BinName has "tv_", "TeamViewer",
    "Other")
| summarize DistinctFamilies = dcount(RmmFamily), Families = make_set(RmmFamily), Binaries = make_set(BinName), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer
| where DistinctFamilies >= 2
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @NewProcessName:(*\\anydesk.exe OR *\\AnyDesk.exe OR *\\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe OR *\\ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe OR *\\ConnectWiseControl.Client.exe OR *\\teamviewer.exe OR *\\TeamViewer.exe OR *\\TeamViewer_Service.exe OR *\\tv_w32.exe OR *\\tv_x64.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(anydesk|screenconnect\.clientservice|screenconnect\.windowsclient|connectwisecontrol\.client|teamviewer|teamviewer_service|tv_w32|tv_x64)\.exe$/i
| case {
    ImageFileName=/anydesk\.exe$/i | RmmFamily := "AnyDesk";
    ImageFileName=/(screenconnect|connectwisecontrol)/i | RmmFamily := "ScreenConnect";
    ImageFileName=/(teamviewer|tv_)/i | RmmFamily := "TeamViewer";
    * | RmmFamily := "Other";
  }
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=[count(field=RmmFamily, distinct=true, as=DistinctFamilies), collect(RmmFamily)])
| DistinctFamilies >= 2

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PraisonAI UI / aiui server listening on 0.0.0.0 (vulnerable exposure) AIWeaponization High
Hunts for launches of the PraisonAI UI / claw dashboard or any host app built on praisonaiui that binds 0.0.0.0 by default and exposes the unauthenticated /api/mcp/connect endpoint. Surfaces the vulnerable server's startup so an analyst can audit network exposure before exploitation. Rationale: Anchors on the exact CLI invocations and Python entry points the advisory names (praisonai ui, praisonai claw, aiui run, praisonaiui.server.create_app, create_host_app, build_host_app). Each of these binds 0.0.0.0 by default per ui.py:114/163/186/204/222 and claw.py:41/93. Cross-checked against GHSA-p75f-6fp4-p57w; non-malicious itself, but every hit is a vulnerable v4.6.48 instance. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p75f-6fp4-p57w
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate AI dev team running praisonai ui on a workstation for agent prototyping
  • CI/CD pipeline running praisonai ui in an ephemeral container for integration tests
  • Internal data-science lab where praisonai is a sanctioned tool
  • Researchers running the upstream PoC on an isolated VM
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("dev-", "lab-", "sandbox-", "ci-"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm praisonai version (run `pip show praisonai` on host) and check whether AUTH_ENFORCE=true is set; if either is true, downgrade severity. Verify the listening socket exposure with `ss -tlnp | grep python` and whether port is reachable from any non-loopback network. Step 2 — Contain: if exposed on a routable interface, immediately firewall the listening port to localhost only, kill the process, and require operator restart with --host 127.0.0.1 plus AUTH_ENFORCE=true. Notify host owner. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot to UC "Child process spawned by PraisonAI UI / aiui" for the same host over the past 30 days to detect prior exploitation; query proxy/WAF logs for inbound POSTs to /api/mcp/connect from any source.

Unauthenticated POST /api/mcp/connect — exploit attempt at web tier AIExploitation High
Hunts for inbound HTTP POSTs to the PraisonAI UI endpoint that converts attacker-controlled JSON (command/args) into a local process launch. Any non-localhost source posting to this exact URI is exploit traffic, since the only documented use is the vulnerable code path itself. Rationale: The advisory names the endpoint praisonaiui/server.py:1488 / line 2770 — POST /api/mcp/connect with a JSON body containing command and args. This URI exists in no other product, so any inbound POST is either the documented PoC or an exploit attempt; no legitimate caller exists besides the vulnerable UI itself. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p75f-6fp4-p57w
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Nessus / Qualys / Tenable / WAS) probing the endpoint as part of an authorised assessment
  • Red-team / pentester running the published PoC during an engagement
  • Sanctioned PraisonAI UI client connecting an MCP server (legitimate operator use, if any)
  • Sourcegraph / GitHub crawler hitting the path from documentation links
Suppression filter
| where not (SourceIP in ("<allow-list of scanner IPs>"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the full POST body from the WAF / reverse proxy. The body field `command` will literally contain the OS binary the attacker asked the server to launch (e.g. /bin/sh, curl, /usr/bin/touch). Cross-reference source IP against threat intel and authorised scanner allow-list. Step 2 — Contain: block the source IP at perimeter, take the PraisonAI host off the network, snapshot disk + memory before reboot. Step 3 — Hunt: on the target host, run the companion UC "Child process spawned by PraisonAI UI / aiui" for the matching timestamp ±2 minutes; check shell histories, /tmp drops, and any new persistence (cron / systemd / Run keys) created by the praisonai service user.

Child process spawned by PraisonAI UI / aiui (post-exploitation RCE) AIInstallation High
Detects any process whose parent command line is a praisonai/aiui host app — meaning the StdioMCPClient successfully invoked an attacker-chosen binary. Any non-Python helper born under this parent is post-exploitation evidence of GHSA-p75f-6fp4-p57w. Rationale: The advisory PoC shows /usr/bin/touch being launched as a child of the praisonai/aiui host process via StdioMCPClient (praisonaiui/features/mcp.py:332). Anchoring on the parent command line listing praisonai/aiui plus a non-Python child is the highest-fidelity post-exploitation signal — the attack literally cannot succeed without producing this parent→child pair. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p75f-6fp4-p57w
ATT&CKT1059 T1190 T1106
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimately configured MCP stdio server tools launched by an authorised operator
  • Subprocess calls from PraisonAI's own agent runtime invoking allowed tool binaries
  • pip/uv install operations running build hooks under the praisonai venv
  • Developer running praisonai ui locally and spawning helper utilities through the chat UI
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip", "uv pip", "setup.py", "build_meta") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "install")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the child binary, its arguments, and SHA256. If the binary is /bin/sh, curl, wget, base64, nc, certutil, or any LOLBin — treat as confirmed exploitation. Capture network destinations the child contacted. Step 2 — Contain: kill the parent praisonai/aiui process tree, isolate the host from network, snapshot memory + disk, rotate any credentials the praisonai service user could read (.env files, ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, cloud metadata IAM role). Step 3 — Hunt: search the host for new persistence (crontab, systemd timers/units, ~/.bashrc, Windows Run keys), outbound C2 over the past 24h from the same `aid`/DeviceId, and any /tmp/* or %TEMP%\* file writes by the praisonai user. Pivot to other hosts running praisonai 4.6.48 with the listener UC.

PraisonAI AgentOS launched with 0.0.0.0 bind exposing unauthenticated /api/chat (CVE-2026-40151) AIWeaponization High
Detects a Python/uvicorn process launching PraisonAI AgentOS or AgentApp with the default `host=0.0.0.0` bind, which exposes the unauthenticated `/api/agents` and `/api/chat` routes named in GHSA-892r-p3jq-jp24. The detection fires on the vulnerable configuration regardless of patch level because v4.5.128 through v4.6.57 still register routes without auth. Rationale: Anchors on the article's named binding (`host: str = "0.0.0.0"`), package import strings (`praisonai`, `AgentApp`, `AgentOS`, `AgentOSConfig`), and the Python/uvicorn launcher implied by the FastAPI deployment. Combining all three string classes in one process record is near-zero FP outside intentional PraisonAI deployments. Cross-checked against: • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/cve-2026-40151-cwe-200-exposure-of-sensitive-infor-41548a8f • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-892r-p3jq-jp24 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/praisonai-cve-2026-44338-auth-bypass.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running PraisonAI locally with --host 0.0.0.0 for container/VM testing
  • Authorized PraisonAI deployment behind nginx/ALB with mTLS terminating in front of the FastAPI app
  • CI/CD smoke-test pipelines launching the vulnerable demo configuration for integration tests
  • Data science notebook environments where 0.0.0.0 is used so Jupyter cells can reach the local service
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "pytest" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--reload" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "\\.tox\\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "site-packages\\pytest"
Response runbook
Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine plus parent (uvicorn? gunicorn? bare python?) and check `pip show praisonai` on the host — anything 4.2.1 ≤ ver ≤ 4.6.57 is vulnerable per the advisory. Identify which agents are registered via `GET /api/agents` from a trusted source. Contain: firewall block inbound to TCP/8000 from non-corporate ranges immediately; coordinate with service owner to either restart with `host=127.0.0.1` or front the service with an authenticating proxy (matches PraisonAI's own hardened deploy-API pattern). Hunt: pivot to UC2 for any historical inbound hits on /api/chat or /api/agents from public IPs; sweep DeviceInfo / IdentityInfo for other hosts running praisonai (`pip ls | grep praisonai` via live response) to find sibling exposed instances.

| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","AgentApp","AgentOS","agentos","AgentOSConfig","AgentAppConfig")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "0.0.0.0"

Unauthenticated POST to PraisonAI /api/chat from external network (CVE-2026-40151 exploitation) AIExploitation Medium
Detects inbound HTTP requests to the PraisonAI AgentOS `/api/chat` or `/api/agents` paths from public/non-corporate sources, optionally without a valid Authorization header. Active in-the-wild scanning of PraisonAI auth-bypass CVEs has been documented within hours of disclosure, so any external hit to these routes is high-fidelity post-compromise reconnaissance or unauthorized agent invocation. Rationale: Anchors directly on the two route strings the advisory's PoV proves are vulnerable (`GET /api/agents`, `POST /api/chat`) plus the default port `8000` and the `python/uvicorn` server process. Joining the inbound network event to a process whose cmdline contains `praisonai` removes the FP risk of any other service that happens to listen on 8000. External-source filter keeps internal pen-test / health-check traffic out. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/praisonai-cve-2026-44338-auth-bypass.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/praisonai-vulnerability-exploited/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4171215/praisonai-vulnerability-gets-scanned-within-4-hours-of-disclosure.html • https://www.brinztech.com/breach-alerts/brinztech-ai-infrastructure-alert-authentication-evasion-broken-access-controls-and-automated-agent-manipulation-the-in-the-wild-scanning-exploitation-loop-of-praisonai-cve-2026-44338
ATT&CKT1190 T1078 T1106
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized external pentest hitting the documented vulnerable endpoint as part of attack-surface validation
  • Vendor-run vulnerability scanners (Qualys, Tenable, Rapid7) issuing CVE-2026-40151 / CVE-2026-44338 detection probes
  • Cloud-provider managed health probes (AWS ELB, GCP LB) hitting /api/agents if mis-configured as a health-check path
  • Internal API gateway that NAT-translates internal traffic to a public-looking egress IP
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP !in (dynamic(["<authorized_scanner_ip_1>","<authorized_scanner_ip_2>"])) and not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pytest","--reload","tests/"))
Response runbook
Triage: was the request answered with HTTP 200 and did the host's PraisonAI version fall in 4.2.1 – 4.6.57? If yes, treat as confirmed unauthorized invocation, not a probe. Pull the request body if WAF logs include it — the `message` field reveals what the attacker asked the agent to do (data exfil prompt, tool invocation, prompt injection chain). Contain: immediate firewall block of the source IP at perimeter; revoke any LLM / vector-DB / tool API keys the deployed agent has access to (they should be considered burned); restart the service bound to 127.0.0.1 behind an authenticating reverse proxy. Hunt: enumerate which agents and tools were registered (config files + `GET /api/agents` response if logged), then audit downstream systems those tools could touch (cloud APIs, vector DB, email integrations, browser-actions) for activity correlating with the inbound timestamps. Sweep for sibling exposed PraisonAI instances using UC1.

Hunts Python processes invoking PraisonAI's AgentTeam/Agents.launch() with a non-loopback bind host, which exposes the unauthenticated GET /{path}/list and POST /{path}[/agent_id] FastAPI routes documented in GHSA-x8cv-xmq7-p8xp. Any external bind of this launch path is functionally a remote unauthenticated agent-execution endpoint. Rationale: Anchors on the exact API names called out in the advisory (AgentTeam.launch / Agents.launch / praisonaiagents) combined with the documented vulnerable default host=0.0.0.0 bind. Cross-checked against the GHSA advisory text and src/praisonai-agents/praisonaiagents/agents/agents.py line references in the report (1923, 2007, 2042, 2086, 2117). Step 1 (triage): Identify the host, user, and full command line; confirm whether the process is listening on a non-loopback interface (netstat / Get-NetTCPConnection on LocalPort from the alert) and whether the AgentTeam path is reachable from outside the host. Step 2 (contain): If the listener is externally reachable, block the listening port at the host firewall and stop the process; have the owner pin praisonaiagents to a patched release or wrap launch() with an auth proxy / bind to 127.0.0.1. Unauthenticated GET /{path}/list and POST hits to PraisonAI agent route AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP traffic to the PraisonAI FastAPI route shape (GET <path>/list, POST <path>, POST <path>/<agent_id>) served by a Python/uvicorn process, with no Authorization header or a non-matching bearer. The advisory confirms the routes accept requests with no Authorization or an arbitrary bearer, so any cross-host hit to this shape is a candidate for unauthenticated agent invocation. Rationale: Pivots on the exact three-route shape registered by AgentTeam.launch (GET {path}/list, POST {path}, POST {path}/{agent_id}) and constrains to hosts where a praisonaiagents-Python process was observed. Inbound IIS/web-proxy view catches the unauthenticated request even when the host log lacks an Authorization header, mirroring the PoV's case names no_auth_list / no_auth_group / wrong_bearer_group / no_auth_per_agent. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x8cv-xmq7-p8xp
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal API gateway or service-mesh health probe hitting /list on the agent port
  • Developer using curl/httpie to test the agent endpoint from another workstation
  • Authorised red-team validating the very GHSA-x8cv-xmq7-p8xp finding
  • Kubernetes liveness/readiness probe configured against the agent listener
  • Internal documentation tools (e.g. Swagger UI bookmarks) issuing the route-shape requests
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("10.0.0.10","10.0.0.11") and csUserAgent !has_any ("kube-probe","GoogleHC","ELB-HealthChecker","Datadog Agent","Pingdom")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the destination host is running PraisonAI and that the request originated from outside the host's loopback; correlate the source IP against known internal automation, reverse-proxy egress IPs, or unknown external scanners. Pull the responding process command line and request body if a WAF/proxy captured it. Step 2 (contain): Restrict the agent port to loopback (firewall rule or relaunch with host=127.0.0.1), front the service with an authenticating reverse proxy, and pin praisonaiagents to a patched release once available. Step 3 (hunt): Search 30 days of proxy/IIS/NGINX logs for any source IP that fetched /list followed by a POST to the same path or to /<agent_id>, then pivot on the responses for sensitive tool / prompt content that may have been exposed; review AgentTeam tool definitions for any with credentials, file-write, or shell-exec capabilities and treat those hosts as scoped incidents.
let PraisonHosts = DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonaiagents","AgentTeam","Agents.launch","praisonai")
  | distinct DeviceId, DeviceName;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("InboundConnectionAccepted","ListeningConnectionCreated","ConnectionSuccess")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","uvicorn.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonaiagents","AgentTeam","Agents.launch","praisonai")
| where LocalPort in (8000,8080,5000,3000,7860,8001) or LocalPort > 1024
| where RemoteIPType in ("Public","Private") and RemoteIP !in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| join kind=inner PraisonHosts on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod in ("GET","POST")
| where (csUriStem endswith "/list" and csMethod == "GET")
   or (csMethod == "POST" and csUriStem matches regex @"^/[A-Za-z0-9_\-]+/?$")
   or (csMethod == "POST" and csUriStem matches regex @"^/[A-Za-z0-9_\-]+/[A-Za-z0-9_\-]+$")
| where scStatus == 200
| where csUserName == "" or isempty(csUserName)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUserAgent, scStatus, csUserName
| summarize Hits = count(), Paths = make_set(csUriStem, 20), UAs = make_set(csUserAgent, 5) by cIP, Computer
| where Hits > 0
| order by Hits desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\python.exe OR *\\python3.exe OR *\\pythonw.exe OR *\\uvicorn.exe) @Initiated:false (@DestinationPort:8000 OR @DestinationPort:8080 OR @DestinationPort:5000 OR @DestinationPort:3000 OR @DestinationPort:7860 OR @DestinationPort:8001) -CIDR(@SourceIp, 127.0.0.0/8)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ConnectionDirection=1
| ContextImageFileName=/python(3|w)?\.exe$|uvicorn\.exe$/i
| LocalPort=8000 OR LocalPort=8080 OR LocalPort=5000 OR LocalPort=3000 OR LocalPort=7860 OR LocalPort=8001
| NOT cidr("127.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/praisonaiagents|AgentTeam|Agents\.launch/i}, field=aid)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, LocalPort, RemoteAddressIP4], function=count())
| _count > 0

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("10b5deab96686f276b8ad71fa4712e1e3d301e4c356812d5d0d595b2b9503ef3", "869564d523c14624afefb211a2e7c6bf8a27b3356bd19a58927fcb5e1ebb014c") or SHA1 in~ ("10b5deab96686f276b8ad71fa4712e1e3d301e4c356812d5d0d595b2b9503ef3", "869564d523c14624afefb211a2e7c6bf8a27b3356bd19a58927fcb5e1ebb014c") or MD5 in~ ("10b5deab96686f276b8ad71fa4712e1e3d301e4c356812d5d0d595b2b9503ef3", "869564d523c14624afefb211a2e7c6bf8a27b3356bd19a58927fcb5e1ebb014c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("10b5deab96686f276b8ad71fa4712e1e3d301e4c356812d5d0d595b2b9503ef3", "869564d523c14624afefb211a2e7c6bf8a27b3356bd19a58927fcb5e1ebb014c") or SHA1 in~ ("10b5deab96686f276b8ad71fa4712e1e3d301e4c356812d5d0d595b2b9503ef3", "869564d523c14624afefb211a2e7c6bf8a27b3356bd19a58927fcb5e1ebb014c") or MD5 in~ ("10b5deab96686f276b8ad71fa4712e1e3d301e4c356812d5d0d595b2b9503ef3", "869564d523c14624afefb211a2e7c6bf8a27b3356bd19a58927fcb5e1ebb014c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["10b5deab96686f276b8ad71fa4712e1e3d301e4c356812d5d0d595b2b9503ef3", "869564d523c14624afefb211a2e7c6bf8a27b3356bd19a58927fcb5e1ebb014c"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
